name: Wei Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at a copper mine, the kind with a big bucket on the front that mucks out the ore after a blast. We go down the decline at six, check the machine, then I spend most of the shift tramming ore from the draw points to the ore pass, back and forth in the dark with my headlights and the radio. I'm eighteen months in and still a bit careful in the tight drives, so the senior guys are faster. The best part is the crew at crib time, sitting on upturned buckets eating whatever someone's mum sent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's your situation?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ana, she's a nurse at the regional hospital. We don't have kids. The underground allowance makes the pay really good, and I've saved about a year's worth because I lived at my parents' place for the first year. There's another underground mine and two open pits within driving distance, so loader drivers are always in demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's the quiet version. Not much changes underground then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the hype was mostly for investors. The mine put a tablet in the crib room two years ago that was meant to plan our shifts better, and it still mostly shows the weather. I might post something sarcastic in the crew group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to finish learning the job properly. My worry is more the usual stuff: rockfalls, dust in my lungs, whether the copper price holds. Plateau or not, underground is still underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it and ask to train on the bigger loader next year, which pays a bit more. I'd keep putting money into the joint account with Ana for a house deposit. Maybe I'd use the chatbot on my phone a bit more for small stuff, like checking my roster pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Ana would be happy I'm not talking about robots at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned dust. How much does the health side weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair bit. My uncle Leo did twenty years underground and coughs every morning now. Leo (my uncle) did twenty years underground at the copper mine and coughs every morning, and that scares me more than any robot does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend on, if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house, honestly. Ana and I have looked at a couple of places near the hospital. We'd probably buy in the next two years.

say: I'd say the **hype** was for investors, like the crib-room tablet showing weather.
I'd post something **sarcastic** in the crew group chat.
think: He gets to **finish learning** the loader job properly.
His real worries are **rockfalls, dust** and the copper price, not AI.
do: Train on the **bigger loader** next year for slightly better pay.
Keep adding to the **house deposit** with Ana.
Use the phone **chatbot** a bit more for small tasks like checking pay.
feel: **Calm**, and glad to keep robots out of dinner conversation.
S0.quote: Leo (my uncle) did twenty years underground at the copper mine and coughs every morning, and that scares me more than any robot does.
fieldNote: His savings and in-demand skill make the plateau **genuinely secure**.
**Health** is his live worry, shaped by his uncle Leo's cough.
He already uses AI **now and then**, but only for small things.

steps.text: Train on the bigger underground loader next year
Keep adding to the house deposit account with Ana
Buy a house near the hospital within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one's closer to what we already see underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we need the union to bargain over every new system, not just robots, because the planning software will change our targets too. With friends I'd say it's not the end of mining. Online I'd share the union's stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think tele-remote loaders are already being tested at mines like ours, where you drive from a room on the surface. That's not a robot taking my job, that's my job moving upstairs. If I'm smart, I can be in that room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for the tele-remote trial the first time they ask. I'd keep the savings where they are and maybe hold off on the house for a year to see where the work goes. I'd go to the union meeting about the new planning software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit worried, a bit curious, because I'd love to not breathe diesel all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes first for you, the robots or the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software. The planning and the ventilation scheduling go first, and then someone up there decides our loader cycle times. The planning software would decide how many buckets I move an hour long before any robot loader takes my seat underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the house. Why, if your savings are good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to know if I'm moving to a remote ops centre in the city. Ana can nurse anywhere, so it's my job that decides where we live. A year of waiting costs us nothing.

say: I'd want the **union** to bargain over **every new system**, not only robots.
I'd tell friends this isn't the **end of mining**.
think: **Tele-remote loaders** move his job upstairs rather than ending it.
He sees a chance to **get into** the remote control room early.
do: Volunteer for the **tele-remote trial** the first time they ask.
Delay the **house purchase** by a year to see where work goes.
Attend the union meeting on the **planning software**.
feel: **Mixed**: some worry, some curiosity about escaping diesel fumes.
S1.quote: The planning software would decide how many buckets I move an hour long before any robot loader takes my seat underground.
fieldNote: He sees software reaching him through **cycle-time targets** before robots.
He links his housing choice to a **possible city move** for remote ops.
His steady style shows: he'd try tech **once it's trialled**, not before.

steps.text: Volunteer for the mine's tele-remote loader trial
Put the house purchase off for one year
Attend the union meeting on the new planning software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for AGI, five for the robots. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this needs government money, fast, like a mining transition fund that pays people while they retrain. I'd sign every petition. At work I'd tell the young guys not to quit yet, because the robots still need a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the remote room I was hoping for would be short-lived too. If AI can drive a remote loader by itself, the room only needs one person watching ten machines. Even the control room I hoped to move into would need one supervisor for ten loaders, and I'm nobody's first choice for supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd talk to Ana and we'd cancel the house plan for now. I'd keep my savings safe and start a proper course, maybe electrical, because someone still has to fix the machines in 2031. In the year after AGI arrives, I'd keep working underground and bank every allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops when I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the time gap between AGI and robots play out for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm mostly hands-on, so I'd probably still have the loader until about 2031. Those three years are my runway. The thinking jobs above me go first, and I watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm okay for now and I've got savings. My dad would tell me to go back to school, and this time I might listen.

say: I'd call for a **mining transition fund** that pays people while they retrain.
I'd tell young miners **not to quit yet**, because robots are a few years away.
think: Even the **remote control room** would shrink to one supervisor for ten loaders.
His **three-year runway** until 2031 is because his job is mostly hands-on.
do: Cancel the **house plan** for now, after talking with Ana.
Start an **electrical course** so he can fix machines after 2031.
Bank **every underground allowance** while the loader job lasts.
feel: **Anxious**, with a stomach drop when he thinks about it.
S2.quote: Even the control room I hoped to move into would need one supervisor for ten loaders, and I'm nobody's first choice for supervisor.
fieldNote: He sees the remote-room hope **collapse** in the fast picture.
His savings and Ana's nursing job give **some control**, so not alarmed.
He'd finally take his **dad's advice** to study.

steps.text: Cancel the house purchase plan with Ana
Enrol in an electrical course at the technical college
Bank every underground allowance into savings
Sign petitions for a mining transition fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side, about eight for the robots. That's more workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at union meetings: we have time to do this properly, so let's not waste it. Retraining deals, transfer rights to the new jobs. With friends I'd be less doom, more planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I can do the tele-remote job for a few years and pick up an electrical ticket on the side. By 2034 I'd want to be the person who fixes the robot loaders, not the one replaced by them. It's a real path, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start the electrical apprenticeship part time, with the mine paying if the union wins that. I'd still buy the house, maybe a cheaper one, because Ana's job is solid. And I'd ask for every tele-remote shift I can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. I can see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our shift boss Jorge, he's 58 and hates screens. Jorge (my shift boss) is 58 and hates screens, and he'd be stuck between too young to retire and too old for a robot room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd ask the company for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid study time. One day a fortnight for the electrical course. If they give that, I'd stay loyal for years.

I'd sound **less doom, more planning** with friends.

fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into a **concrete plan**.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrical apprenticeship in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's nearly a whole career at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind with that much notice. The government should start the transition fund now, while there's time to do it slowly. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think it's honestly fine for me. I'd finish the electrical ticket, work the robots, maybe move to the remote centre. Ten years means I can have kids and a house and still change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house next year as planned. I'd start electrical study in the second year, once things settle at work. Most of all I'd just keep working and saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. Only a bit uneasy about the others on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the ten years change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably have a kid sooner. Ten years of warning means Ana and I could buy the house, have a kid and still have time for me to change trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of this that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old guys. And honestly, the towns. If the robots come and the mines need half the people, the shops and footy clubs go too.

say: With **ten years' notice**, nobody in mining should be left behind.
The government should start a **transition fund** now, while it can go slowly.
think: He sees it as **mostly fine** for him personally.
He can finish an **electrical ticket** and still have a house and kids.
do: Buy the **house next year** as planned.
Start **electrical study** in the second year.
Keep working and **saving** at the same rate.
feel: Close to **calm**, with some unease about **older crewmates**.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning means Ana and I could buy the house, have a kid and still have time for me to change trades.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him keep **family plans** and still change trades.
His remaining worry is **collective**: older workers and mining towns.

steps.text: Buy the house near the hospital next year
Start electrical study in the second year
Start trying for a child with Ana sooner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even my backup plan, the remote room, goes away. What would help is paid study time and a government fund that keeps wages coming while you retrain. My savings buy me a year, but a transition fund would buy the whole town a future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. Robots underground could save lives, and I'm not against that. I just want miners in the room deciding how it happens.

headlineQuote: My savings buy me a year, but a transition fund would buy the whole town a future.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** underground loader operator at a copper mine, eighteen months in.
He lives with Ana, a nurse, and has **a year saved** toward a house.
He'd try **tele-remote** work once it's trialled and uses AI now and then.
He hopes to move **upstairs** to remote operations, then into electrical work fixing robots.
His worry runs from **calm** in the plateau to **anxious** in the two-year AGI picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even the remote control room he hoped for would shrink.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid study time** and a government **fund** that pays wages during retraining.
